scenarios-approach.tldr:
• Triage impact, ask what changed, mitigate first, then investigate with evidence.
  • Capture thread dumps, histograms and previous logs before restarting.
  • Know the toolbox: jcmd, thread dumps, JFR, async-profiler, heap dumps, NMT, kubectl.
  • Answer scenarios as: clarify → mitigate → signals → likely causes → fix → prevent.
scenarios-approach.body:
Senior interviews increasingly ask "production is doing X, what do you do?" They're testing whether you stabilize first, reason from evidence, and know the tools. Use the same structure every time.

The incident loop

  1. Triage (minute 0–2). What's the user impact (error rate, latency, which endpoints, which customers)? Since when? One instance, one zone, or everything? Declare severity and open an incident channel.
  2. Ask "what changed?" Most incidents follow a change: a deploy, config change, feature flag, traffic spike, data growth, dependency deploy, certificate expiry, infrastructure change. Check the deploy log first.
  3. Mitigate before you understand. Roll back the last deploy, turn off the flag, scale out, restart the one bad pod (after capturing evidence), fail over, or shed non-critical traffic. Restoring service is the priority; root cause can wait.
  4. Capture evidence before restarting. Thread dumps, heap histogram, GC log, kubectl logs --previous. A restart destroys the state you need.
  5. Investigate with signals: RED metrics per endpoint (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE per resource (Utilization, Saturation, Errors), traces for the slow path, logs filtered by trace id.
  6. Fix, verify, write the postmortem (blameless): timeline, root and contributing causes, what went well, action items with owners.

The JVM toolbox (keep this in your head)

Question Tool
Which threads burn CPU? top -H -p <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print (the cpu= field), async-profiler, JFR
What are threads waiting on? thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print or jstack <pid>), three dumps a few seconds apart
What's filling the heap? jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram, heap dump (jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file.hprof) + Eclipse MAT
Is GC the problem? GC logs (-Xlog:gc*), jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000, JFR GC events
Native / off-heap memory? Native Memory Tracking: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
Continuous low-overhead profiling JDK Flight Recorder: jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=app.jfr settings=profile
Where does a request spend time? distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry → Tempo/Jaeger)
Container level kubectl top pod, kubectl describe pod (restarts, OOMKilled), kubectl logs --previous, kubectl get events
Shell
# Run these INSIDE the container (or with kubectl exec), where the JVM's pid is usually 1
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 Thread.print > threads-1.txt
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram | head -30
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
kubectl cp order-service-7d9f-abcde:/tmp/heap.hprof ./heap.hprof
# Distroless images have no shell: add an ephemeral debug container sharing the process namespace
kubectl debug -it order-service-7d9f-abcde --image=eclipse-temurin:21-jdk --target=app

How to answer a scenario question in an interview — narrate this order:

  1. Clarify impact and timeline ("is it all endpoints or one? did it start with a deploy?").
  2. Mitigation you'd do right away (rollback/scale/failover) and why.
  3. The signals you'd check, in order, and what each would tell you.
  4. The 3–4 most likely root causes for this symptom and how you'd distinguish them.
  5. The fix, and how you'd prevent recurrence (alert, test, guardrail).

Interview tip saying "first I'd roll back if it correlates with a deploy, but I'd grab a thread dump from one bad pod before it goes" signals real on-call experience more than any tool name.

scenarios-highcpu.tldr:
• Find hot threads with top -H plus thread dumps, or better, a profile (async-profiler, JFR).
  • If GC threads are hot, it's a memory problem.
  • Common causes: tight loops, regex backtracking, busy spinning, heavy serialization or logging, CPU throttling.
  • Bound inputs, add timeouts and keep continuous profiling.
scenarios-highcpu.body:
Symptoms: pods at their CPU limit, latency up across all endpoints, possibly throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total rising), health checks timing out and pods restarting.

First five minutes

  • Is it every instance (traffic or code) or one (a stuck request, a bad node)? Did traffic rise, or did CPU per request rise?
  • Correlates with a deploy → roll back. Traffic spike → scale out / rate limit.
  • Before restarting a hot pod, capture a few thread dumps and a 30-second profile.

Find the hot threads

Shell
# 1. Per-thread CPU inside the JVM process
top -H -p <pid>                      # note the TIDs at the top, e.g. 4721
printf '%x\n' 4721                   # -> 1271 (thread dumps show the native id "nid" in hex)
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > dump1.txt  # find nid=0x1271 and read its stack

# 2. Simpler on JDK 11+: thread dumps include cpu= time per thread. Take two dumps 10 s apart
#    and compare which threads' cpu= grew the most.

# 3. Best: a profile. async-profiler (v3 ships the 'asprof' launcher):
asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu-flame.html <pid>
# or Flight Recorder, then open in JDK Mission Control:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s settings=profile filename=/tmp/cpu.jfr

Read the flame graph: the widest towers are where CPU goes. If the hot threads are G1 Conc#, GC Thread# or VM Thread, it's GC, not your code — go to the memory and GC scenarios.

Common root causes

Cause What you see Fix
Infinite / tight loop one or a few threads at 100% stuck in the same frame across dumps fix the loop condition; add guards
Catastrophic regex backtracking stack in java.util.regex.Pattern$... rewrite the pattern (possessive quantifiers, atomic groups), bound input length, precompile patterns
GC thrashing GC threads hot, heap near max, frequent full GCs see the memory leak / GC scenarios
Busy spin / polling threads in onSpinWait or loops around isEmpty() block on a queue instead of polling
Expensive serialization / logging Jackson or logging frames dominate log less (no huge payloads at INFO), cache ObjectMapper, avoid string building for disabled levels
Hash collisions / bad hashCode HashMap.getNode / TreeNode dominate fix hashCode, validate untrusted keys
Inefficient algorithm on grown data O(n²) loops on lists that used to be small better data structure, pagination, move work to the DB
CPU throttling low usage but high latency; throttling metrics up raise or remove the CPU limit, tune ActiveProcessorCount
Java
// "Does the 12th CSV field start with P?" — '.*' can also match commas, so on a line that
// does NOT match, the engine tries every way to split the line into 11 pieces.
Pattern bad  = Pattern.compile("^(.*,){11}P");
Pattern good = Pattern.compile("^([^,\\r\\n]*,){11}P");   // a field can't contain a comma: linear time

String line = "abc,".repeat(32) + "x";                     // 32 fields, no match
bad.matcher(line).find();    // measured on JDK 21: 28 fields = 2.3 s, 32 fields = 15.6 s, 36 fields = 63 s
good.matcher(line).find();   // well under a millisecond at any of those sizes

Since Java 9 the regex engine memoizes the textbook (a+)+ case, so that classic example no longer hangs. Bounded repetition of greedy wildcards (as above), backreferences and lookarounds still blow up. Make each piece unable to match its own delimiter, cap input length for untrusted strings, and precompile patterns.

Prevent: CPU and throttling alerts per pod, continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Datadog, JFR streaming), load tests with production-sized data, timeouts on request processing, regex review for user-supplied input.

scenarios-memoryleak.tldr:
• A leak shows as heap-after-GC rising over time; peaks alone mean an undersized heap.
  • Enable heap dumps on OOM; diff class histograms; use MAT's dominator tree and path to GC roots.
  • Usual suspects: unbounded caches, ThreadLocals on pool threads, listeners, large Hibernate sessions, high-cardinality metrics.
  • Different OOM messages point to different areas (heap, Metaspace, direct buffers, native threads).
scenarios-memoryleak.body:
Symptoms: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space (or GC overhead limit exceeded) after hours or days; GC frequency rising; latency degrading before the crash; a sawtooth whose lows keep rising.

Leak or just too small? Look at heap usage after full or mixed GCs over time:

  • Post-GC baseline flat but peaks hit the max → the heap is undersized for the load (or a single request allocates a huge object).
  • Post-GC baseline climbs steadily → objects stay reachable: a leak.

First five minutes: restart or scale to restore service, but first make sure you'll get a heap dump. Every JVM should run with:

Shell
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps     # mount a volume; dumps are heap-sized
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError                                   # let Kubernetes restart a broken JVM cleanly
-Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

Diagnose

Shell
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -25    # quick: which classes hold the most bytes? take two, minutes apart, and diff
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof   # full dump (live objects); pauses the JVM, size ≈ used heap

Open the dump in Eclipse MAT:

  1. Leak Suspects report: often names the culprit directly.
  2. Dominator tree: objects sorted by retained size (memory freed if the object were collected). The top entries are usually a big collection.
  3. Path to GC roots (excluding weak/soft references) on the suspect: shows who keeps it alive — a static field, a ThreadLocal on a pool thread, a listener list.

Common leaks in Spring services

Leak Signature in MAT Fix
Unbounded "cache" in a static or singleton HashMap huge HashMap$Node[] held by a singleton bean use a bounded cache (Caffeine maximumSize, TTL)
ThreadLocal not removed on pool threads values held by Thread.threadLocals of http-nio-* threads remove() in finally (filters), or use request-scoped beans
Listeners / callbacks never unregistered growing listener ArrayList unregister, or use weak listeners
Hibernate session holding a long batch StatefulPersistenceContext with millions of entities flush() + clear() every N rows, or StatelessSession
Collecting a whole result set in memory giant ArrayList from a query stream with fetch size, paginate
Metrics with unbounded tags Micrometer meters keyed by user id / URL with ids never use high-cardinality tag values; use URI templates
ClassLoader leak on redeploy (app servers) many copies of the same classes, Metaspace growth stop threads/drivers on undeploy
Java
// LEAK: grows forever, one entry per request
@Component
public class QuoteCache {
    private final Map<String, Quote> byRequestId = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public void remember(String requestId, Quote q) { byRequestId.put(requestId, q); }
}

// FIX: bounded, expiring cache
@Component
public class QuoteCache {
    private final Cache<String, Quote> byRequestId = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(50_000)
        .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
        .recordStats()                                    // expose hit rate via Micrometer
        .build();
    public void remember(String requestId, Quote q) { byRequestId.put(requestId, q); }
}

Other OutOfMemoryError messages and what they mean

Message Area Usual cause
Java heap space heap leak or undersized heap
GC overhead limit exceeded heap >98% time in GC recovering <2% heap (Parallel GC)
Metaspace class metadata class leak, too many generated classes (proxies, Groovy, lambdas in loops)
Direct buffer memory NIO direct buffers Netty/NIO buffers not released; raise -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize only after fixing
unable to create native thread OS threads thread leak (new executors per request), container pid limit
Requested array size exceeds VM limit heap trying to allocate an absurd array (bug)

Prevent: heap-after-GC alert, bounded caches everywhere, load/soak tests (hours, not minutes), heap dumps enabled in every environment.

scenarios-oomkilled.tldr:
• Exit 137 / OOMKilled means the kernel killed the container; no Java error appears.
  • Container memory = heap + Metaspace + thread stacks + code cache + GC structures + direct + native.
  • Use MaxRAMPercentage (~70%) instead of -Xmx equal to the limit; diff NMT summaries to find growth.
  • MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 tames glibc fragmentation.
scenarios-oomkilled.body:
Symptoms: kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137; no Java OutOfMemoryError in the logs; restarts under load.

What's happening: the Linux kernel killed the process because the container exceeded its memory limit. The JVM never got a chance to throw. The JVM's footprint is much more than the heap:

Text
container memory  ≈  heap (-Xmx)
                   + Metaspace (class metadata)
                   + thread stacks (≈1 MB reserved per platform thread; ~200 threads = up to 200 MB)
                   + code cache (JIT, up to 240 MB)
                   + GC structures (G1 remembered sets: often 5–10% of heap)
                   + direct / NIO buffers (Netty, Kafka clients)
                   + native allocations (malloc arenas, compression libs, JNI)

Diagnose

Shell
kubectl describe pod order-service-7d9f-abcde | grep -A5 "Last State"
kubectl top pod order-service-7d9f-abcde                 # current usage vs limit
# Compare JVM view vs container view:
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 VM.flags | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E "MaxHeapSize|MaxRAMPercentage"
# Native Memory Tracking (start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary; ~5% overhead)
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory baseline     # then later:
kubectl exec -it order-service-7d9f-abcde -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary.diff # which category grows?

Common causes and fixes

Cause Fix
-Xmx set close to (or above) the container limit leave 25–35% headroom: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 instead of a fixed -Xmx equal to the limit
No heap setting at all → defaults to 25% of the limit; then someone sets -Xmx = limit use MaxRAMPercentage, never hard-code both
Many platform threads (huge Tomcat pool, executors per request) bound pools; virtual threads for blocking work
Direct buffer growth (Netty, gRPC, Kafka with large batches) fix buffer release; cap with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
glibc malloc arena fragmentation (RSS creeps up, NMT doesn't show it) MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 env var, or jemalloc
Requests == limits set too low for startup spikes profile real usage; set the limit from measurements
YAML
# Kubernetes container spec for a JVM service
resources:
  requests: { memory: "1Gi", cpu: "500m" }
  limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }                 # memory limit = request: predictable scheduling, no surprise OOM from overcommit
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
      -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
      -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
      -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
  - name: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX
    value: "2"

Interview tip the distinction interviewers want: Java OutOfMemoryError = the JVM ran out of a JVM-managed area (you get a stack trace and can get a heap dump); OOMKilled / exit 137 = the kernel killed the whole process for exceeding the cgroup limit (no Java error at all).

scenarios-gc.tldr:
• Read GC logs: Full GCs, evacuation failures and humongous allocations signal trouble.
  • Reduce allocation and live data before tuning flags.
  • Leave heap headroom; set a pause goal; consider ZGC for latency-critical services.
  • Long pauses also trigger Kafka rebalances and health-check failures.
scenarios-gc.body:
Symptoms: periodic p99/p999 spikes of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds; timeouts in callers; Kafka consumers kicked out of the group; health checks failing intermittently; jvm_gc_pause_seconds_max spiking.

Read the GC log (enable it everywhere: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags)

Text
[12.345s][info][gc] GC(311) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1834M->412M(4096M) 18.402ms     <- healthy
[95.210s][info][gc] GC(530) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 3010M->2950M(4096M) 61.2ms
[96.004s][info][gc] GC(531) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure) 4012M->4090M(4096M) 412.5ms   <- no room to copy
[96.880s][info][gc] GC(532) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 4090M->2900M(4096M) 2873.110ms              <- the problem
Pattern in the log Meaning Typical fix
Young pauses grow over time survivor/old copying grows with live data reduce allocation, check for a leak
Pause Full in G1 concurrent cycle couldn't keep up; heap exhausted more heap, find the leak, lower InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent, reduce allocation rate
(Evacuation Failure) (older JDKs: To-space exhausted) no free regions to copy survivors into more headroom, larger heap
G1 Humongous Allocation objects ≥ half a region (e.g. 4 MB+ arrays with 8 MB regions) allocated directly in old gen avoid giant arrays/buffers (stream, chunk), or raise -XX:G1HeapRegionSize
Low heap occupancy but long pauses time-to-safepoint problems, swapping, CPU throttling check -Xlog:safepoint, disable swap, fix CPU limits
Frequent young GCs with short pauses very high allocation rate cut allocation (avoid boxing, big temporary collections, excessive logging)
Shell
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000          # every second: survivor/eden/old/metaspace %, YGC/FGC counts and times (abridged)
#  S0     S1     E      O      M     YGC   YGCT    FGC   FGCT
#  0.00 100.00  63.21  97.85  94.10  1830  41.2     12   31.9    <- old gen ~98% and full GCs piling up

Fix options, in order

  1. Reduce garbage and live data: fix leaks, stream instead of materializing, cache smarter, avoid per-request huge buffers. This beats any flag.
  2. Right-size the heap: G1 needs headroom; running at 90%+ occupancy after GC guarantees trouble.
  3. Set a pause goal: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 (G1 adapts young gen size to meet it).
  4. Switch collector for latency-critical services: ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC, generational by default from JDK 23; on JDK 21 add -XX:+ZGenerational) keeps pauses under ~1 ms regardless of heap size, at some throughput and memory cost.
  5. Use JFR (jdk.GarbageCollection, jdk.ObjectAllocationSample) to find which code allocates the most.

Kafka-specific consequence: a stop-the-world pause longer than max.poll.interval.ms or the session timeout triggers a rebalance and duplicate processing, so GC problems often show up first as "Kafka keeps rebalancing".

scenarios-latency.tldr:
• If latency correlates with a deploy, roll back first, then diff versions.
  • Compare traces to find the span that grew: DB, downstream call or in-process.
  • Usual culprits: N+1, missing index, new sync call, cache key change, allocation-driven GC, pool changes.
  • Prevent with canaries, version-split dashboards and query-count tests.
scenarios-latency.body:
Symptoms: dashboards show p99 from 120 ms to 300 ms (p50 barely moved) right after release 1.42 went out; error rate normal.

First five minutes: the change is the prime suspect, so roll back (or shift the canary back to 0%). If latency recovers, you have a clean A/B: diff the versions. If it doesn't, it wasn't the deploy — look for another change (traffic mix, a dependency's release, data growth).

Narrow it down

Tools: traces sorted by duration for the affected endpoint (look at the span waterfall), per-endpoint latency histograms by version label, DB slow query log since the deploy, JFR/async-profiler from a canary vs a baseline pod, git diff v1.41..v1.42.

Frequent culprits

Culprit Clue Fix
N+1 queries introduced by a new association access trace shows dozens of tiny DB spans per request fetch join / @EntityGraph / batch fetching
Query on a new column without an index one DB span grew; EXPLAIN shows full scan add the index (online), fix the query
New synchronous downstream call new HTTP span in the trace make it async, cache it, or parallelize with CompletableFuture
Cache key or serializer changed cache hit ratio dropped at deploy time restore key compatibility, warm the cache
More allocation → GC pauses GC pause time up on new pods profile allocations, fix hot path
Pool sizes changed in config pending acquisitions on Hikari or executors restore / right-size
Logging at INFO of full payloads CPU in logging, disk I/O log ids, not bodies; async appender

Prevent: canary releases with automated latency comparison (Argo Rollouts / Flagger analysis), performance tests in CI on critical endpoints, query-count assertions in tests, dashboards split by version.

scenarios-threadpool.tldr:
• All request threads busy with low CPU means threads are blocked waiting.
  • Group thread-dump stacks to see the bottleneck: DB pool, socket reads, locks or futures.
  • Timeouts on every outbound call are non-negotiable.
  • Bulkheads and circuit breakers stop one dependency from consuming all threads.

scenarios-connpool.tldr:
• Use Hikari metrics: long usage time means connections are held too long; long acquire time means demand exceeds the pool.
  • Leak detection logs who holds connections; the DB shows long and idle-in-transaction sessions.
  • Biggest causes: remote calls inside @Transactional, slow queries, lock contention, Open Session in View.
  • Grow the pool only within the database's capacity.
scenarios-connpool.body:
Symptoms: errors like SQLTransientConnectionException: shop-db - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms; latency jumps to exactly the connectionTimeout; Micrometer shows hikaricp_connections_active = max and hikaricp_connections_pending > 0.

The pool is a symptom. Connections are being held too long or there are too few for the demand. Find out which.

Metric / signal Interpretation
hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds (time a connection is held) high slow queries or long transactions
hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds high, usage normal genuine demand > pool size
DB shows many sessions idle in transaction (PostgreSQL) / Sleep with open trx (MySQL) the app holds a transaction open while doing something else
Leak detection warnings code borrows a connection and never returns it
DB lock waits queries blocked by another transaction's locks
Properties
# Find the code that holds connections too long: Hikari logs a stack trace of the borrower
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000
SQL
-- PostgreSQL: who is holding connections, and what are they doing?
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS trx_age, wait_event_type, wait_event, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'shop' ORDER BY trx_age DESC NULLS LAST;
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 60) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

-- MySQL: long transactions and lock waits
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, trx_mysql_thread_id, trx_query FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started;
SELECT * FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits\G

Root causes I've seen most often

  1. Remote calls inside @Transactional: the method opens a transaction (and a connection), then calls a slow HTTP service or Kafka send().get(). Every slow call pins a connection.
Java
// BAD: connection held for the whole remote call
@Transactional
public Order place(OrderRequest r) {
    Order o = orders.save(Order.from(r));
    PaymentResult p = paymentClient.charge(r.payment());   // 2 s remote call holding a DB connection
    o.markPaid(p.id());
    return o;
}

// BETTER: keep DB work in short transactions; do remote work outside them
public Order place(OrderRequest r) {
    Order o = tx.execute(s -> orders.save(Order.from(r)));        // TransactionTemplate: short
    PaymentResult p = paymentClient.charge(r.payment());           // no connection held
    return tx.execute(s -> orders.markPaid(o.getId(), p.id()));    // short again (or use the outbox pattern)
}
  1. Slow query after data growth (missing index) — every request holds its connection longer.
  2. Lock contention — a batch job updating many rows blocks request transactions.
  3. Open Session in View (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, the default) keeps a connection bound for the whole web request including view rendering and serialization. Set it to false.
  4. Pool too small for real concurrency — but only increase it after ruling out the above, and within the database's total connection budget.

Mitigation: kill the long-running blocker (pg_terminate_backend(pid) / KILL <id>), pause the batch job, roll back the change that introduced the slow path. Keep connection-timeout short (1–3 s) so the system fails fast instead of piling up threads.

scenarios-dbslow.tldr:
• Find top statements by total time (pg_stat_statements, performance_schema digests).
  • Kill or disable the offending source first; add indexes online.
  • Common causes: missing index after growth, plan regression, N+1, unbounded queries, batch jobs on the primary.
  • Prevent with statement timeouts, query review and production-sized load tests.
scenarios-dbslow.body:
Symptoms: DB CPU pinned, query latency up across services, connection pools filling up everywhere, replicas lagging.

First five minutes: identify the top statements by total time; if one new query dominates, kill/disable its source (feature flag, roll back, pause the batch job). Consider failing reads over to replicas if they're healthy.

SQL
-- PostgreSQL: who is burning the CPU right now, and who blocks whom
SELECT query, calls, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time, 1) AS mean_ms, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

SELECT pid, state, now() - query_start AS running_for, wait_event_type, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY running_for DESC;

SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, left(blocking.query, 60) AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY (pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid));
SQL
-- PostgreSQL (needs pg_stat_statements): top queries by total execution time
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time, 1) AS mean_ms, rows, left(query, 100)
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Currently running, longest first
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS running, state, left(query, 100) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY running DESC;
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(12345);      -- cancel the query; pg_terminate_backend kills the session

-- MySQL 8: top statement digests
SELECT digest_text, count_star, round(sum_timer_wait/1e12, 1) AS total_s, round(avg_timer_wait/1e9, 1) AS avg_ms
FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 10;
SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;   -- then KILL QUERY <id>;

Common root causes

Cause Clue Fix
Missing index exposed by data growth top query does full scans; rows examined huge add the index online (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY / MySQL online DDL)
Plan regression same query suddenly slower; plan changed after stats update ANALYZE, extended statistics, query rewrite; pin via hints only as a last resort
N+1 or chatty access after a release call counts exploded, mean time tiny fix the access pattern in the app
Unbounded queries SELECT * ... without LIMIT from a new admin endpoint paginate, limit, move to a replica/warehouse
Batch job or report on the primary heavy aggregation queries run on a replica, throttle, schedule off-peak
Lock pile-up many sessions waiting on locks, CPU from spinning find and kill the blocker; shorter transactions
Cache outage traffic that Redis used to absorb now hits the DB restore cache, protect DB with rate limits

Prevent: slow query alerting, pg_stat_statements/digest dashboards, query review in code review, load tests with production-sized data, statement timeouts (SET statement_timeout, MySQL max_execution_time), read replicas for reporting.

scenarios-deadlock.tldr:
• Thread dumps report Java-level deadlocks; stuck latches, futures and leaked permits need pattern spotting across dumps.
  • Fix with lock ordering, tryLock timeouts and timeouts on every wait.
  • A deadlock health indicator turns silent hangs into alerts.
  • DB lock waits look like hangs: find the blocker and keep transactions short.
scenarios-deadlock.body:
Symptoms: a subset of requests never complete; throughput drops to zero for some operations; threads accumulate; no errors logged (nothing is failing, everything is waiting).

Java-level deadlock

Shell
jcmd 1 Thread.print | grep -A 30 "Found one Java-level deadlock"
Text
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"pool-3-thread-2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f1c... (object 0x00000000e5a1..., a com.shop.Account),
  which is held by "pool-3-thread-1"
"pool-3-thread-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f1c... (object 0x00000000e5b2..., a com.shop.Account),
  which is held by "pool-3-thread-2"

The JVM detects deadlocks involving synchronized monitors and java.util.concurrent locks (ownable synchronizers). It can't detect waits that never complete for other reasons: a CountDownLatch that's never counted down, a Future.get() without a timeout on a task that's stuck in a queue (thread-starvation deadlock), a semaphore permit leak. For those, look for many threads parked on the same object across several dumps.

Fixes: consistent lock ordering, tryLock with timeouts, never call external code while holding a lock, separate executors for dependent stages, timeouts on every wait (await(timeout), get(timeout)).

Java
// Health indicator that turns silent deadlocks into a visible DOWN status
@Component
public class DeadlockHealth implements HealthIndicator {
    private final ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
    @Override public Health health() {
        long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();
        if (ids == null) return Health.up().build();
        return Health.down().withDetail("deadlockedThreads",
            Arrays.stream(mx.getThreadInfo(ids)).map(ThreadInfo::getThreadName).toList()).build();
    }
}

Database-level deadlocks and lock waits — the database resolves true deadlocks by aborting one transaction (MySQL error 1213, PostgreSQL deadlock detected), so those surface as errors, not hangs. Lock waits behind a long-running transaction do look like hangs:

SQL
-- MySQL 8
SELECT waiting_pid, waiting_query, blocking_pid, blocking_query, wait_age FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits;
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G          -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event_type, left(query, 80) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';

Fix the blocker (often a forgotten open transaction, a migration, or a batch job), keep transactions short, order row access consistently, and set lock_timeout / innodb_lock_wait_timeout so waits fail fast.

scenarios-cascading.tldr:
• Missing timeouts plus layered retries turn one slow service into a platform outage.
  • Mitigate by stopping retries, opening circuit breakers, degrading features and shedding load.
  • Prevent with timeout budgets, single-layer retries with jitter, bulkheads and fallbacks.
  • Liveness probes must never depend on other services.

scenarios-kafkalag.tldr:
• Even lag on all partitions means slow consumers; lag on one points to a hot key or poison pill.
  • Frequent rebalances mean processing time exceeds max.poll.interval.ms or GC pauses.
  • Speed up with batch listeners, bulk lookups and bulk writes.
  • Alert on lag growth and message age; dead-letter poison pills.
scenarios-kafkalag.body:
Symptoms: kafka_consumergroup_lag climbing; downstream data stale (emails late, search index behind); sometimes rebalance logs every few minutes.

Shell
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group order-indexer
# PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG      CONSUMER-ID
# 0          18234011        18234020        9        indexer-1
# 1          17110432        17998213        887781   indexer-2      <- one partition way behind
# 2          18011567        18011580        13       indexer-3

Read the lag pattern

Pattern Likely cause Fix
All partitions lagging evenly consumers too slow overall, or producer rate jumped profile processing; batch DB writes; scale consumers up to the partition count; add partitions (plan for key remapping)
One partition far behind hot key (one big customer) or a poison pill retried forever on that partition spread the key (composite key), dead-letter the bad record, check the error handler
Lag resets / duplicates, frequent rebalances processing time > max.poll.interval.ms, GC pauses, slow startup lower max.poll.records, speed up processing, static membership, cooperative rebalancing
Lag stuck, no consumer assigned consumers crashed / group empty check pods, logs, auth errors, deserialization failures
Lag grows only at night batch producers flooding autoscale consumers on lag (KEDA)

Typical slow-processing culprit

Java
// SLOW: one DB round trip + one HTTP call per record, sequentially
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders")
public void on(OrderEvent e) {
    Customer c = customerClient.get(e.customerId());   // 40 ms
    repo.save(Index.of(e, c));                          // 5 ms
}

// FASTER: batch listener, bulk lookups, bulk writes
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", batch = "true")
public void on(List<OrderEvent> events) {
    Map<Long, Customer> customers = customerClient.getAll(events.stream().map(OrderEvent::customerId).collect(toSet()));
    repo.saveAll(events.stream().map(e -> Index.of(e, customers.get(e.customerId()))).toList());   // JDBC batching on
}

Prevent: alert on lag growth and on time-lag (age of the oldest unprocessed message), not on absolute offsets; dead-letter topics for poison pills; consumer processing-time metrics; capacity tests at peak producer rates.

scenarios-cache.tldr:
• A hit-ratio collapse is either Redis being unavailable or the cache being bypassed (keys changed, mass expiry, eviction).
  • Protect the DB first: rate limit, serve stale data, coalesce requests.
  • Make cache failures fast with short timeouts and a circuit breaker.
  • Version key prefixes and warm caches before switching.
scenarios-cache.body:
Symptoms: latency and DB load jump together; keyspace_hits / (hits + misses) drops from 95% to near zero; errors like RedisConnectionFailureException or QueryTimeoutException; or no Redis errors at all but every lookup misses after a deploy.

Two different incidents with the same symptom

  1. Redis unavailable (node failure, failover, network, memory full): every cache read fails, often slowly (connection timeouts), adding latency on top of DB load.
  2. Cache bypassed: a deploy changed key format or serializer, a mass expiry (cache avalanche), a FLUSHALL, or eviction because maxmemory was reached.

Mitigate

  • Protect the database first: rate-limit expensive endpoints, serve stale or partial data, enable request coalescing.
  • If Redis is down: make cache calls fail fast (short command timeout, circuit breaker around Redis) so requests go straight to the DB instead of waiting on timeouts.
  • If a deploy broke keys: roll back, then warm the cache before re-releasing.
Shell
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E "keyspace_(hits|misses)|evicted_keys|expired_keys"
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|mem_fragmentation_ratio"
redis-cli --latency            # live latency sampling
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10       # slow commands (KEYS *, big HGETALL, etc.)

Design fixes

  • Treat the cache as optional: wrap reads in a circuit breaker; on failure go to the DB (with a rate limit).
  • Short timeouts on the Redis client (spring.data.redis.timeout=200ms).
  • TTL jitter to avoid synchronized expiry; mutex/single-flight rebuild for hot keys (see Redis → cache failure modes).
  • Versioned key prefixes (v2:product:42) so a format change doesn't read incompatible data, plus warm-up of the new version before switching.
  • Monitor hit ratio, evictions and memory as first-class SLOs.

scenarios-deployfail.tldr:
• Errors right after a deploy: roll back first, investigate second.
  • Typical causes: config or secrets, schema mismatch, dependency conflicts, contract changes, optimistic readiness.
  • Use kubectl logs --previous and pod events to see why containers died.
  • Prevent with canaries, backward-compatible migrations, validated config and dependency convergence.
scenarios-deployfail.body:
Symptoms: 5xx rate jumps from 0.1% to 15% within minutes of a rollout; maybe only on new pods; maybe pods crash-looping.

First minute: roll back. Don't debug forward while users fail. With Kubernetes: kubectl rollout undo deployment/order-service (or revert in Argo CD / abort the canary). Then investigate calmly.

What breaks on deploy, and the tell-tale signs

Cause Signal
Missing or wrong config / secret startup fails, CrashLoopBackOff, Could not resolve placeholder, auth errors to dependencies
Schema mismatch SQLSyntaxErrorException: Unknown column, Hibernate validation errors: migration not run, or code deployed before/after the migration it needs
Dependency version conflict NoSuchMethodError, ClassNotFoundException, NoClassDefFoundError at runtime (two versions of a library on the classpath)
Incompatible API / event contract consumers throwing deserialization errors; 400s from a downstream
Readiness probe too optimistic errors only in the first minute of each pod: traffic arrives before caches/pools/JIT are warm
Resource limits too tight OOMKilled or CPU throttling only in the new version
Feature flag defaulting on new code path enabled for everyone
Shell
kubectl rollout status deployment/order-service
kubectl get pods -l app=order-service                       # CrashLoopBackOff? restarts?
kubectl logs deploy/order-service --previous | head -50      # why the last container died
kubectl describe pod <pod> | sed -n '/Events/,$p'            # probe failures, OOMKilled, image pull errors
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core     # find conflicting library versions

Safe-deploy practices that prevent most of this

  • Canary or progressive delivery with automatic rollback on error-rate/latency analysis.
  • Backward-compatible changes: expand/contract database migrations, tolerant readers for events and APIs, never remove a field in the same release that stops writing it.
  • Readiness that means ready: a readiness group that includes warm-up; startupProbe for slow starters.
  • Config validated at startup (@ConfigurationProperties + @Validated) so bad config fails the rollout instead of the 10,000th request.
  • Dependency convergence checks (Maven Enforcer dependencyConvergence) and a BOM.

scenarios-resources.tldr:
• Disk full: rotate logs, keep dumps on volumes, check lsof +L1 for deleted-but-open files.
  • Too many open files: find leaked sockets/streams; reuse HTTP clients.
  • Port exhaustion: pool connections with keep-alive instead of opening one per request.
  • DNS and clock skew cause intermittent timeouts and token validation failures.
scenarios-resources.body:
The "boring" resource limits cause a surprising share of outages.

Disk full

  • Signs: No space left on device, database refusing writes, Kafka brokers going offline, log writes failing (sometimes silently), pods evicted for ephemeral-storage.
  • Diagnose: df -h, du -xh / --max-depth=2 | sort -h | tail, lsof +L1 (deleted files still held open — space isn't freed until the process closes them).
  • Usual causes: logs without rotation, heap dumps written to the container filesystem, temp files not cleaned, Kafka retention set too long, DB binlogs/WAL piling up (a stuck replica or replication slot).
  • Fix: rotate and cap logs (logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-history, total-size-cap), ship logs to stdout, set ephemeral-storage limits, alert at 80%.

Too many open files

Shell
cat /proc/<pid>/limits | grep "open files"     # the limit
ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l                       # current count
lsof -p <pid> | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head    # what kind: sockets? files?

Causes: leaked streams or sockets (missing try-with-resources), a new HTTP client created per request (each with its own pool), too-low ulimit -n. Fix the leak; reuse clients; raise limits for brokers and databases.

Ephemeral port exhaustion / TIME_WAIT

  • Signs: Cannot assign requested address / BindException on outbound connections under load.
  • Cause: opening a new TCP connection per request without keep-alive; each closed connection sits in TIME_WAIT for ~60 s.
  • Diagnose: ss -s, ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l.
  • Fix: connection pooling with keep-alive in HTTP clients, reuse RestClient/WebClient beans, tune pool sizes.

DNS failures and slowness

  • Signs: UnknownHostException, intermittent 5-second delays (a DNS timeout and retry), errors after a service's IP changed.
  • Java caches successful lookups (networkaddress.cache.ttl, 30 s default without a security manager) and negative lookups (10 s). Kubernetes ndots:5 makes every external name try several search domains first.
  • Fix: use fully qualified names with a trailing dot for external hosts or lower ndots, enable NodeLocal DNSCache, keep connection pools warm so lookups are rare.

Clock skew: JWT validation failing with "token not yet valid", TLS errors, wrong ordering in logs. Ensure NTP/chrony runs everywhere; allow small leeway in JWT validation.

qa.q: A service's p99 latency doubled after a deployment. Walk me through it.
qa.a: Check whether it correlates with the deploy across all instances; if so, roll back or shift the canary back to restore service, keeping one pod for evidence. Then compare traces of slow requests between versions to see which span grew (DB, a downstream call, or in-process time), check DB slow logs and query counts (N+1, missing index), cache hit ratio, GC pause time and pool saturation on the new pods, and diff the code and config. Fix, add a performance test or query-count assertion, and add version-split dashboards.

qa.q: CPU is at 100% on one pod only. What do you do?
qa.a: Capture evidence first: per-thread CPU with top -H or two thread dumps comparing cpu= times, plus a 30-second async-profiler or JFR profile. If the hot threads are GC threads it's a memory problem; if it's application threads stuck in one frame it's likely a loop, regex backtracking or one pathological request. Then restart or drain that pod, fix the cause, and add a timeout or input limit so one request can't burn a core forever.

qa.q: How do you find a memory leak in a Java application?
qa.a: Confirm it's a leak by watching heap usage after GC climb over time. Take class histograms minutes apart and diff them, then a heap dump and open it in Eclipse MAT: check Leak Suspects, sort the dominator tree by retained size, and follow the path to GC roots to find what keeps the objects alive (a static map, a ThreadLocal, a listener list). Fix with bounded caches or proper cleanup, and run soak tests.

qa.q: What's the difference between Java OutOfMemoryError and a pod being OOMKilled?
qa.a: OutOfMemoryError is thrown by the JVM when a JVM-managed area (heap, metaspace, direct memory) can't satisfy an allocation; you get a stack trace and can get a heap dump. OOMKilled (exit 137) means the Linux kernel killed the process because total container memory exceeded the cgroup limit, often because heap plus non-heap memory (threads, metaspace, direct buffers, native) was larger than the limit; there's no Java error. Fix by leaving headroom with MaxRAMPercentage and measuring native memory with NMT.

qa.q: All Tomcat threads are busy but CPU is low. What's going on?
qa.a: Threads are blocked waiting, not working: on a slow downstream HTTP call without a timeout, on database connections from an exhausted pool, or on a lock. Take a few thread dumps and group the request threads by top frame to see what they wait on. Mitigate by opening circuit breakers or restarting, then add timeouts, bulkheads and circuit breakers so one dependency can't hold every thread.

qa.q: How do you prevent cascading failures in microservices?
qa.a: Timeouts on every remote call with budgets that shrink downstream, retries only at one layer with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget, circuit breakers with fallbacks, bulkheads per dependency, load shedding and rate limits at the edge, async communication for non-critical paths, liveness probes that don't depend on other services, and graceful degradation of features.

qa.q: Kafka consumer lag is growing on only one partition. Why?
qa.a: Most likely a hot key sending far more records to that partition, or a poison-pill record that fails and is retried forever, blocking the partition. It can also be a consumer instance that's slower (bad node, GC). Check the error logs and DLT for that partition, the key distribution, and the processing time of that consumer; fix with a dead-letter policy, a better key or more parallelism for that key.

qa.q: Your pods restart every few hours with exit code 137. How do you investigate?
qa.a: Confirm OOMKilled in kubectl describe pod. Compare the JVM's configured heap and the container limit; check whether heap after GC grows (heap leak) or RSS grows while the heap is stable (native memory). Enable Native Memory Tracking and diff summaries over time to find the growing category (threads, direct buffers, metaspace, malloc arenas). Fix the leak or the sizing, e.g. MaxRAMPercentage around 70, bounded thread pools, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, and alert on memory headroom.

qa.q: How do you debug "Connection is not available, request timed out" from HikariCP?
qa.a: Look at Hikari metrics: if connection usage time is high, connections are held too long (slow queries, long transactions, remote calls inside @Transactional, open-in-view); if acquisition time is high with normal usage, demand exceeds the pool. Enable leak detection to log where connections are held, check the database for long or idle-in-transaction sessions and lock waits, then fix the holder. Increase the pool only within the database's capacity.

qa.q: What would you put in a postmortem?
qa.a: A summary of impact (who, how long, how bad), a timeline from detection to resolution, the root cause and contributing factors, what went well and what didn't (detection, tooling, communication), and concrete action items with owners and dates. Blameless: focus on systems and process, not individuals.

qa.q: A database migration locked a table and the site went down. How do you prevent it?
qa.a: Use online DDL (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, MySQL ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE or INSTANT, gh-ost/pt-osc for rebuilds), expand/contract for column changes, set a low lock timeout so the migration gives up instead of queuing all traffic behind it, run migrations separately from deploys during low traffic, check for long-running transactions first, and test migrations against production-sized data.

qa.q: Why should you capture a thread dump before restarting a hung service?
qa.a: The dump shows what every thread was doing at the moment of the hang (blocked on a lock, waiting for a connection, stuck in a socket read), which is usually the only evidence of the root cause. A restart clears it and the problem returns later. Take two or three dumps a few seconds apart to distinguish stuck threads from slow ones.

cheat.scenarios-cheatsheet:
How to handle an incident (and answer scenario questions)

  • Triage impact, ask what changed, mitigate first, then investigate with evidence.
  • Capture thread dumps, histograms and previous logs before restarting.
  • Know the toolbox: jcmd, thread dumps, JFR, async-profiler, heap dumps, NMT, kubectl.
  • Answer scenarios as: clarify → mitigate → signals → likely causes → fix → prevent.

Scenario: CPU at 100% on a Java service

  • Find hot threads with top -H plus thread dumps, or better, a profile (async-profiler, JFR).
  • If GC threads are hot, it's a memory problem.
  • Common causes: tight loops, regex backtracking, busy spinning, heavy serialization or logging, CPU throttling.
  • Bound inputs, add timeouts and keep continuous profiling.

Scenario: heap keeps growing until OutOfMemoryError

  • A leak shows as heap-after-GC rising over time; peaks alone mean an undersized heap.
  • Enable heap dumps on OOM; diff class histograms; use MAT's dominator tree and path to GC roots.
  • Usual suspects: unbounded caches, ThreadLocals on pool threads, listeners, large Hibernate sessions, high-cardinality metrics.
  • Different OOM messages point to different areas (heap, Metaspace, direct buffers, native threads).

Scenario: pods restart with OOMKilled (exit code 137)

  • Exit 137 / OOMKilled means the kernel killed the container; no Java error appears.
  • Container memory = heap + Metaspace + thread stacks + code cache + GC structures + direct + native.
  • Use MaxRAMPercentage (~70%) instead of -Xmx equal to the limit; diff NMT summaries to find growth.
  • MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 tames glibc fragmentation.

Scenario: long GC pauses and latency spikes

  • Read GC logs: Full GCs, evacuation failures and humongous allocations signal trouble.
  • Reduce allocation and live data before tuning flags.
  • Leave heap headroom; set a pause goal; consider ZGC for latency-critical services.
  • Long pauses also trigger Kafka rebalances and health-check failures.

Scenario: p99 latency doubled after a deploy

  • If latency correlates with a deploy, roll back first, then diff versions.
  • Compare traces to find the span that grew: DB, downstream call or in-process.
  • Usual culprits: N+1, missing index, new sync call, cache key change, allocation-driven GC, pool changes.
  • Prevent with canaries, version-split dashboards and query-count tests.

Scenario: all Tomcat threads busy, requests timing out

  • All request threads busy with low CPU means threads are blocked waiting.
  • Group thread-dump stacks to see the bottleneck: DB pool, socket reads, locks or futures.
  • Timeouts on every outbound call are non-negotiable.
  • Bulkheads and circuit breakers stop one dependency from consuming all threads.

Scenario: "Connection is not available, request timed out"

  • Use Hikari metrics: long usage time means connections are held too long; long acquire time means demand exceeds the pool.
  • Leak detection logs who holds connections; the DB shows long and idle-in-transaction sessions.
  • Biggest causes: remote calls inside @Transactional, slow queries, lock contention, Open Session in View.
  • Grow the pool only within the database's capacity.

Scenario: database CPU at 100% and every query is slow

  • Find top statements by total time (pg_stat_statements, performance_schema digests).
  • Kill or disable the offending source first; add indexes online.
  • Common causes: missing index after growth, plan regression, N+1, unbounded queries, batch jobs on the primary.
  • Prevent with statement timeouts, query review and production-sized load tests.

Scenario: the service hangs (Java or database deadlock)

  • Thread dumps report Java-level deadlocks; stuck latches, futures and leaked permits need pattern spotting across dumps.
  • Fix with lock ordering, tryLock timeouts and timeouts on every wait.
  • A deadlock health indicator turns silent hangs into alerts.
  • DB lock waits look like hangs: find the blocker and keep transactions short.

Scenario: one slow service takes down the whole platform

  • Missing timeouts plus layered retries turn one slow service into a platform outage.
  • Mitigate by stopping retries, opening circuit breakers, degrading features and shedding load.
  • Prevent with timeout budgets, single-layer retries with jitter, bulkheads and fallbacks.
  • Liveness probes must never depend on other services.

Scenario: Kafka consumer lag keeps growing

  • Even lag on all partitions means slow consumers; lag on one points to a hot key or poison pill.
  • Frequent rebalances mean processing time exceeds max.poll.interval.ms or GC pauses.
  • Speed up with batch listeners, bulk lookups and bulk writes.
  • Alert on lag growth and message age; dead-letter poison pills.

Scenario: Redis goes down (or the cache hit ratio collapses)

  • A hit-ratio collapse is either Redis being unavailable or the cache being bypassed (keys changed, mass expiry, eviction).
  • Protect the DB first: rate limit, serve stale data, coalesce requests.
  • Make cache failures fast with short timeouts and a circuit breaker.
  • Version key prefixes and warm caches before switching.

Scenario: errors spike right after a deploy

  • Errors right after a deploy: roll back first, investigate second.
  • Typical causes: config or secrets, schema mismatch, dependency conflicts, contract changes, optimistic readiness.
  • Use kubectl logs --previous and pod events to see why containers died.
  • Prevent with canaries, backward-compatible migrations, validated config and dependency convergence.

Scenario: disk full, too many open files, port exhaustion, DNS failures

  • Disk full: rotate logs, keep dumps on volumes, check lsof +L1 for deleted-but-open files.
  • Too many open files: find leaked sockets/streams; reuse HTTP clients.
  • Port exhaustion: pool connections with keep-alive instead of opening one per request.
  • DNS and clock skew cause intermittent timeouts and token validation failures.
